title: Milarepa's remorse
hookLine: Milarepa used black magic to take revenge, then turned to the teaching in remorse

cards: A saint Tibetans hold dear begins his life story having caused many deaths. That isn't a rumor; it's how the story itself tells it. Milarepa was a boy when his father died.

His uncle and aunt took charge of the family's fields and house, promising to hand them back when the boy grew up. They didn't. The widow and her children were left to work as servants on their own land, in rags.
His mother never forgot it. And when Milarepa was grown, she put a demand to him that would change everything.

teach.h: BLACK MAGIC, AT HIS MOTHER'S DEMAND.
teach.b: His mother sent him to learn black magic, and told him, in the story, that if he failed she would take her own life. He learned it.
At the uncle's house, during a wedding feast, the building collapsed and many guests died, though the uncle and aunt survived. His mother rejoiced.
When the villagers turned against her, he called down a hailstorm on their fields. Then the turn.
The biography says he was filled with remorse: he couldn't sleep, couldn't eat, couldn't stop seeing what he had done.

In Buddhist teaching, actions, karma, bring their results, and he knew that what he had set in motion would follow him. But his remorse didn't stop at guilt, which can just sit on a person. It got up and went looking.

He sought out a teacher, then another, and finally heard the name Marpa, and the story says the name alone moved him to tears. Why start there? Tibetans could have told the life of a saint who was always good.
Instead they keep the worst part in, at the start, in full.
As teachers tell it, the message is plain: no one is too far gone to turn back. The harm is real, and the story never pretends otherwise. But the turn is real too.
Milarepa will spend years paying for what he did.

how: Milarepa's life story is read and retold in Tibetan Buddhist communities, and teachers use its opening, revenge and remorse, to show that even serious wrongdoing can be turned from through regret, purification and practice.

o: a curse his mother laid on the uncle's family
the guilt that kept him hiding in a cave
sorrow over his harm that sent him seeking a teacher

p: no sleep, no food, then a search

s: Milarepa's biography leaves out his crimes to protect his name
it keeps them in, at the start, in full.
his remorse led him to search for a teacher
it didn't stop at guilt; it sent him looking, finally to Marpa.
Milarepa's mother regretted the revenge too
in the story she rejoiced. the remorse was his.

games.q: you're Milarepa. your revenge has worked: the house has fallen and the fields are ruined. your mother is celebrating. what do you do?
o: celebrate with her; justice is done.
try to forget it and move on.
let the remorse send you to find a teacher.
games.why: Milarepa couldn't sleep or eat for remorse, and went looking for a teacher, finally finding Marpa.

practice: Without digging for anything heavy, let one small harm you've been causing lately come to mind, a sharp tone, a habit, a word about someone behind their back, and name it plainly.
If there's a sting, let it be there; then picture yourself turning, the way a person turns on a road, and setting that one harm down.

wordCard.voice: Milarepa's remorse. The sorrow over his revenge that didn't stop at guilt, but sent him looking for a teacher. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit for regret; in some Abhidharma lists it can be wholesome or not, depending on what it regrets.

carryVoice: Your line: he turned back. Remorse that went looking is where his road began. Day nine hundred seventy-two.

sources.ref: The Life of Milarepa (Tsangnyön Heruka), the early chapters
